lead: Every receiver adds its own noise, so a weak signal enters with one signal-to-noise ratio and leaves with a worse one. Noise figure says how much worse, the Friis cascade formula shows that the first stage with gain decides most of it, and sensitivity turns the result into the weakest signal the receiver can use. Phones, Wi-Fi routers and satellite receivers are all specified with these three numbers, and they close the link budget that starts with the Friis transmission equation.
prereq: You need: decibels (dB and dBm) and the link budget from antenna fundamentals.

sections.h3: Noise factor, noise figure and noise temperature

blocks.text: A resistor at temperature T delivers available noise power kTB into a matched load over a bandwidth B. Here k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann's constant and T is in kelvin. At the standard reference temperature T₀ = 290 K, kT₀ = 4.00 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz, which is −174 dBm in 1 Hz.
A two-port block (amplifier, mixer or filter) adds noise of its own, so its output signal-to-noise ratio is lower than its input ratio. The noise factor compares the two:

blocks.where: both ratios are power ratios in the same bandwidth, with the source at T₀ = 290 K. F is a plain number and F ≥ 1 for any real block.

blocks.text: Noise figure is the same quantity in decibels, NF = 10 log₁₀ F, and back again F = 10<sup>NF/10</sup>. A block with F = 2 has NF = 3.01 dB. Noise temperature says the same thing in kelvin: T<sub>e</sub> = (F − 1)T₀, so an amplifier with NF = 2 dB (F = 1.585) has T<sub>e</sub> = 0.585 × 290 = 170 K. Satellite receivers are quoted in kelvin because T<sub>e</sub> adds directly to the antenna's noise temperature T<sub>A</sub>.
A passive lossy part at T₀ (a cable, filter or switch) with loss L as a power ratio has G = 1/L and F = L. Its noise figure equals its loss in dB, and its noise temperature is (L − 1)T₀.

blocks.where: F is the noise factor of the whole chain; F₁, F₂, F₃ are the stage noise factors and G₁, G₂ the available power gains, all linear ratios, never dB.

blocks.text: Read it as noise referred to the input. Stage 1 counts in full. Stage 2's extra noise (F₂ − 1) is divided by G₁, because stage 1 has already amplified the signal by G₁ before stage 2 adds anything. Stage 3 is divided by G₁G₂ and is usually tiny. The same formula in kelvin is T<sub>e</sub> = T<sub>e1</sub> + T<sub>e2</sub>/G₁ + T<sub>e3</sub>/(G₁G₂) + …

items: Convert every noise figure to a linear factor, F = 10<sup>NF/10</sup>.
Convert every gain to a linear power ratio, G = 10<sup>G(dB)/10</sup>; a loss L dB gives G = 10<sup>−L/10</sup>.
Put the linear numbers into the Friis formula.
Convert back with NF = 10 log₁₀ F.

blocks.text: The design rule follows at once: put a low-noise amplifier with real gain first. A lossy part in front of the LNA adds its whole loss to the system noise figure, because the LNA's noise is then divided by G = 1/L, which is less than one. The same part after 20 dB of gain barely shows.

sections.h3: Sensitivity and the receiver noise floor

blocks.text: Sensitivity is the weakest input that still gives the demodulator the signal-to-noise ratio it needs. Start from the thermal noise in the channel, add the receiver's own noise, then add the required SNR:

blocks.where: P<sub>min</sub> is in dBm; −174 dBm/Hz is kT₀; B is the noise bandwidth of the channel in Hz; NF is the receiver noise figure in dB; SNR<sub>min</sub> is the demodulator's requirement in dB. The first three terms are the input-referred noise floor.

blocks.text: Every factor of 10 in bandwidth costs 10 dB: a 10 MHz channel's floor is −104 dBm before NF is added. With SNR<sub>min</sub> = 0 dB the formula gives the minimum detectable signal (MDS).

When the antenna sees a sky or ground cooler than 290 K, work in kelvin instead: the system noise temperature is Tsys = TA + Te, the noise floor is kTsysB, and the sensitivity is that floor plus SNRmin. Sensitivity sets the weak end of the receiver's range; the strong end is set by compression and intermodulation (see nonlinearity).

examples.question: A receiver chain has an LNA (G₁ = 15 dB, NF₁ = 2 dB), a mixer (G₂ = 10 dB, NF₂ = 12 dB) and an IF amplifier (G₃ = 20 dB, NF₃ = 10 dB). Find the cascaded noise figure and noise temperature, and the sensitivity in a 10 MHz channel when the demodulator needs SNR = 10 dB.
steps: Linear noise factors: F₁ = 10<sup>0.2</sup> = 1.585; F₂ = 10<sup>1.2</sup> = 15.85; F₃ = 10<sup>1.0</sup> = 10.
Linear gains: G₁ = 10<sup>1.5</sup> = 31.62; G₂ = 10<sup>1.0</sup> = 10. G₃ is not needed: nothing follows the last stage.
examples.answer: NF = 3.19 dB (F = 2.083, T<sub>e</sub> = 314 K) and P<sub>min</sub> = −90.8 dBm. The mixer and IF amplifier together add only 1.2 dB to the LNA's 2 dB, because the LNA's 15 dB gain divides their noise by 31.6 and more.

examples.question: A satellite receiver's antenna has T<sub>A</sub> = 100 K. A cable with 2 dB loss at 290 K connects it to an LNA (NF = 1 dB, G = 20 dB), followed by the rest of the receiver with NF = 10 dB. Find the receiver noise temperature, the system noise temperature and the sensitivity in 1 MHz for SNR<sub>min</sub> = 8 dB. How much does moving the LNA to the antenna, ahead of the cable, gain?
steps: Noise floor: kT<sub>sys</sub>B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 430 × 10⁶ = 5.94 × 10⁻¹⁵ W = −112.3 dBm; P<sub>min</sub> = −112.3 + 8 = −104.3 dBm.
examples.answer: Cable first: T<sub>e</sub> = 330 K, T<sub>sys</sub> = 430 K, P<sub>min</sub> = −104.3 dBm. LNA at the antenna: T<sub>e</sub> = 118 K, P<sub>min</sub> = −107.2 dBm, 2.9 dB better, which is why masthead LNAs exist.

traps: Adding noise figures in dB. 2 dB followed by 12 dB is not 14 dB; convert to linear factors, use Friis, convert back (the answer is 3.19 dB).
Putting dB gains in the Friis denominators. G₁ must be 31.62, not 15.
Forgetting a lossy part in front. A 2 dB cable before the LNA adds 2 dB straight onto the system figure; behind a 1 dB LNA with 20 dB of gain it adds about 0.02 dB.
Using −174 dBm as the noise power. It is per hertz: always add 10 log₁₀B with B in Hz.
Adding the antenna temperature to F. T<sub>A</sub> adds to T<sub>e</sub> in kelvin; NF is defined with the source at 290 K.

quiz.q: Define noise figure and write the relation between noise factor and noise temperature.
quiz.a: NF = 10 log₁₀F with F = SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub> for a source at T₀ = 290 K. T<sub>e</sub> = (F − 1)T₀, or F = 1 + T<sub>e</sub>/T₀.

quiz.q: Why does the first stage decide most of the cascaded noise figure?
quiz.a: Each later stage's added noise is divided by the total gain ahead of it when referred to the input: (F₂ − 1)/G₁, (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂). A first stage with large gain makes those terms small, leaving F₁.

quiz.q: A 3 dB filter sits in front of an amplifier with NF = 1.5 dB. Find the system noise figure.
quiz.a: Filter: F = 2, G = 0.5. Amplifier: F = 10<sup>0.15</sup> = 1.413. F = 2 + 0.413/0.5 = 2.826, NF = 4.51 dB: the 3 dB loss plus the 1.5 dB amplifier.

quiz.q: A receiver has B = 200 kHz, NF = 6 dB and needs SNR<sub>min</sub> = 9 dB. Find its sensitivity.
A 3 dB filter and a 15 dB, 2 dB-NF LNA are used in either order. Compare the two noise figures of the pair.
quiz.a: Filter first: F = 2 + (1.585 − 1)/0.5 = 3.17, NF = 5.01 dB. LNA first: F = 1.585 + (2 − 1)/31.62 = 1.617, NF = 2.09 dB. The LNA-first order is 2.9 dB better, but the filter must then protect the LNA from strong out-of-band signals some other way.

beyond: Not for the exam. Noise figure is measured by the Y-factor method: a calibrated noise source switches between two temperatures, and the ratio of the two output powers gives F. Radio-astronomy receivers are cooled to cut T<sub>e</sub> to a few kelvin. Search for 'Y-factor method' and 'G/T figure of merit'.
